title: Impact of ABO Blood System on Immunogenicity and Vaccine Efficacy of COVID-19 Booster Vaccination-A Population-Based Study of 3066 Individuals.

analysis.research_question_and_background: ABO blood group has been associated with SARS‐CoV‐2 susceptibility, but little data exist regarding its impact on breakthrough infections and antibody responses following booster vaccination.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This multicenter, population‐based cohort study included individuals ≥ 18 years who received a SARS‐CoV‐2 booster vaccination, with 3066 participants (mean age 49 [35–59], 62% female) analyzed in multivariable regression models.
analysis.methods: Antibody levels against SARS‐CoV‐2 receptor binding domain (RBD) and neutralizing antibodies against wild‐type and Omicron variant were assessed at baseline, after 4 weeks, and after 6 months; time‐dependent Cox regression analysis was used to evaluate breakthrough infection rates.
analysis.main_results: No association was found between anti‐RBD/neutralizing antibodies and ABO or Rh(D) type 4 weeks post‐booster; AB blood group had significantly lower breakthrough infection rates (HR 0.67 [0.50–0.90]; p = 0.008) compared to O, with a trend for group B (HR 0.82 [0.66–1.01]; p = 0.06); no associations were observed with Rh(D) or COVID‐19 severity.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors conclude that ABO or Rh(D) blood group was not associated with COVID‐19 severity or antibody responses, but differences in ABO group appear relevant for Omicron transmission, despite not supporting previously discussed protective effects of anti‐A/B/Rh(D) agglutinins.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Findings suggest ABO blood group may influence Omicron transmission risk, potentially informing targeted vaccination strategies or surveillance approaches, though no impact on vaccine-induced immunity or disease severity was observed.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's population-based design and large sample size provide moderate evidence strength, though limitations include reliance on self-reported blood types and potential residual confounding factors not fully adjusted in models.

analysis.summary_en: This population-based cohort study investigated the impact of ABO and Rh(D) blood groups on COVID-19 booster vaccine immunogenicity and breakthrough infections in 3066 adults. While no associations were found between blood groups and antibody responses or disease severity, AB blood group showed significantly lower breakthrough infection rates compared to O group, with a similar trend for group B. The findings suggest ABO blood type may influence Omicron transmission risk but not vaccine-induced immunity, providing insights for potential targeted public health strategies.

title: Impact of Non-Pharmaceutical Interventions Targeted at COVID-19 Pandemic on Influenza Burden-A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

analysis.scope_and_question: This review examines the impact of non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) implemented during the COVID-19 pandemic on the global burden of seasonal influenza. The study focuses on quantifying changes in influenza incidence between pre-pandemic and intra-pandemic periods across diverse populations and settings.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted following PRISMA guidelines within the RESPINOW project. The search screened 20,676 records, ultimately including 115 studies from 98 countries that reported absolute influenza case counts before and during the pandemic. Data extraction and quality assessment used a modified NHLBI tool for before-after studies, with influenza cases normalized by reporting period length and relative changes estimated using incidence rate ratios.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The COVID-19 pandemic was associated with an unprecedented global reduction in influenza incidence, with a decline of −92% (95% CI: −94 to −90). Reductions were observed across all transmission zones and WHO regions, with larger decreases in high-income countries (−96%, 95% CI: −98 to −94) compared to low-income settings (−82%, 95% CI: −88 to −73). Age-specific declines were smaller among young children (<6 years: −66%) than adults aged 18–64 years (−80%), and influenza A appeared to decline more strongly than influenza B.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review highlights data limitations and the need for robust epidemiological indicators to better understand the impact of NPIs on influenza. While geographic variations were observed (e.g., near-elimination in some countries versus −61% in South Korea), the reasons for these differences remain unclear. The study also noted that the impact on young children was less pronounced than in other age groups, warranting further investigation.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Strengthened, integrated global surveillance systems are needed to inform future pandemic responses and better assess the impact of public health interventions. The findings underscore the importance of developing robust epidemiological indicators to monitor respiratory virus circulation during and after pandemics, particularly in low-income settings where data may be limited.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review and meta-analysis quantified the impact of COVID-19-related non-pharmaceutical interventions on global influenza burden. Analyzing 115 studies from 98 countries, researchers found an unprecedented 92% reduction in influenza incidence during the pandemic period. The decline varied geographically, with high-income countries experiencing greater reductions (96%) than low-income settings (82%). Age-specific analysis showed smaller decreases in young children (<6 years: 66%) compared to adults (18–64 years: 80%), and influenza A declined more strongly than influenza B. The study highlights the need for strengthened global surveillance systems to better understand and monitor the effects of public health interventions on respiratory virus circulation during future pandemics.

title: Effect of probiotics on humoral responses to COVID-19 vaccination in older adults: a randomized, placebo-controlled trial (PIRATES-COV study).

analysis.research_question_and_background: Although COVID-19 vaccination has reduced morbidity and mortality, adults aged 65 y old and older are at high risk of complications from COVID-19. Few studies have evaluated the potential benefit of probiotic supplementation in this context in this high-risk population.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This study was a randomized controlled trial recruiting adults between 65 and 89 y of age living in Quebec, Canada, who received an mRNA booster (Pfizer-BioNTech or Moderna). Participants provided dried blood spot samples at baseline, at 3- and 6-month post-vaccination.
analysis.methods: Probiotic supplementation (Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus Rosell®-11 and Lacticaseibacillus paracasei Rosell®-215, 1x6x10^9 CFU per capsule) versus placebo was administered from 15 d pre- to 15 d post-vaccination. The primary outcome was the proportion of participants without detectable anti-S1-receptor binding domain (anti-S1-RBD) antibodies at 6 months post-vaccination.
analysis.main_results: 592 adults were enrolled. At 6 months post-vaccination, anti-S1-RBD antibodies were comparable between groups, and the percentage of participants with undetectable antibody response in the placebo and probiotic groups (1.2% vs 1.6%) was comparable. Anti-N seropositivity was lower in the probiotic group at 6 months (OR 0.6, 95% CI 0.4-0.9; p = 0.02) and marginally lower at 3 months after adjustment.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Probiotic supplementation administered around COVID-19 vaccination did not change the proportion of seronegative participants for anti-S1-RBD antibodies at 6 months. However, in the probiotic group, anti-N antibody levels were lower, while self-reported COVID-19 infections also tended to be reduced, although this difference was not statistically significant.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that probiotic supplementation may not enhance humoral responses to COVID-19 vaccination in older adults, but may reduce anti-N antibody levels and potentially lower COVID-19 infection incidence, warranting further investigation.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence strength is moderate due to the randomized controlled design and large sample size, but the study is limited by the speculative interpretation of reduced anti-N antibody levels and self-reported infection data without virological confirmation.

analysis.summary_en: This randomized controlled trial investigated the effect of probiotics on humoral responses to COVID-19 vaccination in older adults (65-89 years) in Quebec, Canada. Participants received either a probiotic supplement (Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus Rosell®-11 and Lacticaseibacillus paracasei Rosell®-215) or placebo from 15 days pre- to 15 days post-vaccination with an mRNA booster. The primary outcome was the proportion of participants without detectable anti-S1-RBD antibodies at 6 months. Results showed no significant difference in anti-S1-RBD antibody levels between groups, but anti-N seropositivity was lower in the probiotic group at 6 months (OR 0.6, 95% CI 0.4-0.9; p = 0.02). Self-reported COVID-19 infection incidence was 16.5% overall, with a non-significant reduction in the probiotic group (13.9% vs 19.1% placebo). The study concludes that probiotic supplementation did not enhance humoral responses but may reduce anti-N antibody levels and potentially lower infection risk.

title: Convalescent Plasma Restores Viral Clearance After Anti-Spike Monoclonal Antibody Failure in Immunocompromised COVID-19 Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Individual Patient Data.

analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on SARS-CoV-2 in immunocompromised patients with persistent viraemia following anti-Spike monoclonal antibody (mAb) therapy, examining whether convalescent plasma (CCP) restores viral clearance.

analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Prioritizing CCP as a treatment option for immunocompromised patients with mAb-resistant SARS-CoV-2 infections, with attention to optimizing transfusion volume.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review and meta-analysis examines the efficacy of convalescent plasma (CCP) in immunocompromised patients with persistent SARS-CoV-2 viraemia following anti-Spike monoclonal antibody (mAb) therapy. The study found that CCP transfusion led to viral clearance in 70.2% of cases, with a positive association between total CCP volume transfused and clearance. The evidence base includes 47 cases (30 published, 17 unpublished) from 2020 to 2026. The review highlights CCP as a viable treatment option for mAb-resistant infections but notes limitations in sample size and lack of long-term outcome data.

title: Timing, Titre, and Host Determinants of Convalescent Plasma Efficacy in COVID-19: A Systematic Review With Design-Stratified Narrative Synthesis.

analysis.scope_and_question: The review examines the efficacy of convalescent plasma (CP) in COVID-19, focusing on three interacting determinants: timing, antibody titre, and host characteristics. The central question is whether conflicting outcomes from large randomized trials can be reconciled through these factors.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: A systematic review with design-stratified narrative synthesis (PRISMA 2020; SWiM; OSF: https://osf.io/tjcuq) was conducted. PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus were searched through May 2026. Thirty-one studies (20,793 patients; 8 RCTs, 23 observational) were included, using a standardized 91-field extraction matrix.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: CP is effective only under specific conditions: early administration, sufficient antibody titre, and use in seronegative or immunocompromised hosts who have not mounted an endogenous antibody response. Among RCTs, 4 of 6 found benefit with earlier timing, 3 of 4 with higher-titre CP, and two large RCTs (n = 12,522) showed preferential benefit in seronegative recipients. Modelling estimates suggest CP saved tens of thousands of lives in the US during the first pandemic year when deployed early.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Conflicting results from large randomized trials initially led to recommendations against routine CP use. A significant gap exists in the assessment of non-IgG immunoglobulins, with only 2 of 31 studies reporting IgA or IgM data, despite evidence of their potent neutralizing activity against SARS-CoV-2.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Findings reframe CP efficacy as a conditional question, providing a template for precision deployment of passive immunotherapy in future pandemics. There is a need for systematic assessment of antibody classes (IgA, IgM) in CP products to optimize therapeutic efficacy.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review reconciles conflicting evidence on convalescent plasma (CP) efficacy in COVID-19 by identifying three critical determinants: timing, antibody titre, and host characteristics. CP is effective only when administered early, with sufficient titre, to seronegative or immunocompromised patients. Among 31 studies (20,793 patients), RCTs confirmed these conditions, with modelling suggesting CP saved tens of thousands of lives when deployed early. A major evidence gap exists in the assessment of non-IgG immunoglobulins (IgA, IgM), with only 2 of 31 studies reporting such data. The findings reframe CP efficacy as conditional and provide a template for precision passive immunotherapy in future pandemics.

title: DNA oligonucleotides block viral entry of SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variants

analysis.research_question_and_background: Successful viruses including SARS-CoV-2 antagonize and evade immune detection to establish infection, and as population immunity to the ancestral strain has risen, new variants—particularly Omicron—have evolved to avoid detection by both circulating antibodies and the innate immune system.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study explored the sensitivity of Omicron BA.1 to diverse innate stimuli and investigated the antiviral activity of DNA oligonucleotides against SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variants.
analysis.methods: Mechanistic studies were conducted using genetic and pharmacological assays to determine the effect of short and long DNA oligonucleotides on Omicron infection, and in vivo experiments were performed to assess the reduction of SARS-CoV-2 Omicron titers.
analysis.main_results: Omicron variants are uniquely restricted by small DNA oligonucleotide ligands known to activate TLR9, and short DNA oligonucleotides of diverse sequences block Omicron infection at the entry step downstream of TMPRSS2-mediated activation, with activity confirmed to be independent of TLR9.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings identify a previously unrecognized antiviral activity of short DNA oligonucleotides and establish them as selective inhibitors of SARS-CoV-2 Omicron entry.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These oligodeoxynucleotides (ODNs) are active in vivo, reducing SARS-CoV-2 Omicron titers, which suggests potential therapeutic applications against Omicron variants.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study demonstrates high evidence strength with mechanistic and in vivo validation, though the generalizability to all Omicron subvariants and long-term effects requires further investigation.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the antiviral activity of DNA oligonucleotides against SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variants. The researchers found that Omicron BA.1 is uniquely sensitive to small DNA oligonucleotide ligands, which block viral entry at a step downstream of TMPRSS2-mediated activation, independent of TLR9. Short DNA oligonucleotides of diverse sequences were effective, while longer ones were not. In vivo experiments confirmed that these oligodeoxynucleotides reduce SARS-CoV-2 Omicron titers, establishing them as selective inhibitors. This discovery highlights a novel antiviral mechanism with potential therapeutic implications against Omicron variants.

title: Effectiveness of BNT162B2 and CoronaVac vaccines in reducing COVID-19 severity among children aged 3-4 years in Brazil.

analysis.research_question_and_background: National population-based databases from large countries can provide real-world estimates of COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness. This analysis examined the effectiveness of BNT162b2 and CoronaVac against severe COVID-19-related outcomes in children aged 3 to 4 years during the Omicron phase of the pandemic in Brazil.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This nationwide population-based cohort study assessed incidence rate ratios for hospitalization due to COVID-19-associated severe acute respiratory syndrome, invasive ventilatory support, and death among children aged 3 to 4 years, according to vaccination status (unvaccinated, 1 dose, or 2 doses), during 2022-2023.
analysis.methods: Data on laboratory-confirmed COVID-19-related hospitalizations, clinical outcomes, and vaccination status were obtained from OpenDATASUS, and vaccination coverage was estimated using data from the Brazilian Ministry of Health COVID-19 vaccination dashboard.
analysis.main_results: The study period spanned epidemiological weeks 31-52 of 2022 and weeks 1-13 of 2023. Among children aged 3 to 4 years, completion of the primary series increased to 15% for CoronaVac and 2% for BNT162b2 during the study period, corresponding to 797,956 and 79,650 individuals receiving the second dose, respectively. A total of 963 children were hospitalized with COVID-19-associated severe acute respiratory syndrome.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: COVID-19 vaccination, predominantly based on the CoronaVac vaccine, was associated with a significant reduction in severe outcomes among children aged 3-4 years, providing robust evidence to support pediatric immunization strategies and public health efforts.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Vaccine effectiveness against hospitalization was 79.0% (95% CI, 69.9%-85.4%) after partial vaccination and 49.2% (95% CI, 32.5%-61.9%) after completion of the primary series (p < 0.01). Effectiveness against invasive mechanical ventilation was 77.6% and 79.1%, respectively; no deaths occurred among fully vaccinated children.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Direct comparisons between vaccines were not feasible because of the lower proportion of BNT162b2 recipients. The evidence strength is moderate due to the observational design and potential confounding factors, though the large population-based sample enhances reliability.

analysis.summary_en: This nationwide population-based cohort study evaluated the effectiveness of BNT162b2 and CoronaVac vaccines in reducing severe COVID-19 outcomes among children aged 3-4 years in Brazil during the Omicron phase (2022-2023). The study analyzed hospitalization rates, invasive ventilatory support, and mortality based on vaccination status. Results showed that partial vaccination with CoronaVac provided 79.0% effectiveness against hospitalization, while full series completion offered 49.2% effectiveness. No deaths occurred among fully vaccinated children. Despite the significant reduction in severe outcomes, direct vaccine comparisons were limited due to lower BNT162b2 uptake. The findings support pediatric COVID-19 vaccination as a strategy to reduce severe disease burden.

title: Uptake of COVID‐19 Vaccines and Intention to Vaccinate in the Democratic Republic of the Congo: A Cross‐Sectional Survey

The review underscores persistent suboptimal vaccine uptake in Sub-Saharan Africa and calls for strategies that address demographic disparities, enhance trust in health authorities, and utilize trusted communication channels to improve vaccination coverage.

title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Antivirals for COVID-19 in the Post-vaccine, Omicron Era: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.

analysis.scope_and_question: This review evaluates the effectiveness of nirmatrelvir-ritonavir and molnupiravir against hospitalization and death in vaccinated populations during the post-Omicron era of COVID-19.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: A systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (from January 2020) and observational studies (from January 2022) in vaccinated adults, searching PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane library, with random-effects meta-analysis and subgroup analysis by age and study quality.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: RCTs in vaccinated populations did not demonstrate reduced hospitalization or death with nirmatrelvir-ritonavir or molnupiravir; observational studies suggested nirmatrelvir-ritonavir benefit but not molnupiravir; RCTs for nirmatrelvir-ritonavir had limited statistical power.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Mixed results for molnupiravir mortality (OR = 0.61; 95% CI .41-.91; HR = 0.65; 95% CI .42-1.01); observational studies showed benefit for nirmatrelvir-ritonavir but not molnupiravir; RCTs lacked power to detect clinically important differences.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Further research is needed to clarify antiviral effectiveness in vaccinated populations; observational data suggest potential benefit for nirmatrelvir-ritonavir but require confirmation.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluates the effectiveness of nirmatrelvir-ritonavir and molnupiravir in vaccinated populations during the post-Omicron COVID-19 era. The analysis included 43 studies (8 RCTs, 35 observational). RCTs did not demonstrate reduced hospitalization or death with either antiviral, though nirmatrelvir-ritonavir RCTs had limited statistical power. Observational studies suggested benefit for nirmatrelvir-ritonavir but not molnupiravir. Molnupiravir showed mixed mortality results. The findings highlight the need for further research to clarify antiviral effectiveness in vaccinated populations and the importance of considering study limitations when interpreting results.

title: Sociodemographic and Health-Risk Determinants of COVID-19 Vaccine Booster Preferences and Willingness to Pay in Singapore: Discrete Choice Experiment.

analysis.scope_and_question: This study focuses on COVID-19 vaccine booster preferences and willingness to pay in the general population of Singapore, aiming to identify sociodemographic and health-risk determinants influencing booster acceptance.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: A discrete choice experiment survey was conducted among 1567 participants from an online panel in Singapore in June 2022, using a 2-stage design and mixed logit model to analyze preferences for booster characteristics and willingness to pay.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Respondents preferred boosters with longer protection duration, especially under higher COVID-19 risks, and were willing to pay S$1.43 per percentage-point increase in effectiveness and S$4.95 per additional month of protection. Sociodemographic factors like younger age, female gender, non-Chinese ethnicity, higher socioeconomic status, and chronic conditions were associated with higher booster acceptance.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The study did not address potential regional variations within Singapore or explore the impact of prior COVID-19 infection on booster preferences beyond the identified negative association. Long-term behavioral changes and evolving public perceptions were not examined.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Policymakers should tailor booster strategies and communication to address sociodemographic disparities and health-risk attitudes, focusing on groups with lower acceptance rates like older adults, those with lower education, and individuals with prior infection to improve uptake and ensure sustainable immunization coverage.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines COVID-19 booster preferences in Singapore using a discrete choice experiment. It found that the general population prefers boosters with longer protection duration, particularly under higher COVID-19 risks, and is willing to pay for increased effectiveness and extended protection. Sociodemographic factors such as younger age, female gender, non-Chinese ethnicity, higher socioeconomic status, and chronic conditions were linked to higher booster acceptance, while older adults, those with lower education, and individuals with prior infection were less likely to accept boosters. The findings suggest that targeted strategies and communication efforts are needed to address these disparities and improve booster uptake for sustainable long-term immunization coverage.

title: Post-COVID-19 rise in central precocious puberty: an integrative Review

analysis.scope_and_question: This review examines the association between the COVID-19 pandemic and an increase in central precocious puberty (CPP), particularly among girls, focusing on epidemiological findings, clinical features, and proposed mechanisms.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: This is a narrative review that synthesizes epidemiological findings, clinical features, and proposed mechanisms related to the rise in CPP during the COVID-19 pandemic.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The available evidence supports a reproducible epidemiological signal of increased CPP during the pandemic, particularly in girls, but does not establish a single causal mechanism. Proposed mechanisms include sedentary behavior, weight gain, increased screen exposure, sleep disruption, psychological stress, altered healthcare-seeking behavior, and environmental endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs).
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: While high-throughput toxicology data suggest that some environmental compounds can activate human KISS1R- or GnRHR-related signaling, pediatric exposure levels, internal dose, target-tissue concentrations, and disease-level causality remain unproven. The female predominance and limited mean BMI shift in pandemic-era CPP are not fully explained by current hypotheses.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: A cautious integrative model is proposed to reconcile observed patterns, including the strong female predominance and temporal association with lockdown-related exposures. Future research should prioritize cohort studies, exposure assessments, and mechanistic studies to test these hypotheses.

analysis.summary_en: This narrative review examines the post-COVID-19 rise in central precocious puberty (CPP), particularly among girls. It synthesizes epidemiological evidence showing a reproducible increase in CPP during the pandemic period, though without establishing a single causal mechanism. The review explores multiple potential factors including sedentary behavior, weight gain, increased screen time, sleep disruption, psychological stress, altered healthcare-seeking behavior, and environmental endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs). While some environmental compounds have shown potential to activate puberty-related signaling in experimental systems, concrete evidence for their role in pandemic-era CPP remains lacking. The authors propose an integrative model to reconcile observed patterns and emphasize the need for future cohort, exposure, and mechanistic studies to better understand this phenomenon.

title: Epidemiology and mortality among hospital-acquired cases of COVID-19 in the pre-Omicron and Omicron periods: A data-linkage study in Victoria, Australia.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addressed the public-health problem of hospital-acquired COVID-19 by asking why in-hospital infections carry higher risks than community-acquired cases and whether this changed between pre-Omicron and Omicron periods.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective cohort study was conducted in Victoria, Australia, linking state surveillance systems to identify COVID-19 hospitalisations from January 2021 to June 2024, classifying episodes as hospital-acquired if the first positive test occurred at least eight days after admission.
analysis.methods: Age, sex, intensive care unit admission and 30-day mortality were compared between hospital-acquired and non-hospital-acquired cases across pre-Omicron and Omicron periods using linked surveillance data.
analysis.main_results: Among 6,485 hospital-acquired and 62,670 non-hospital-acquired episodes, median age was 77.8 versus 77.6 years before Omicron and 52.6 versus 73.1 years during Omicron; monthly hospital-acquired cases rose to 21% under Omicron, and case fatality rates were higher for hospital-acquired cases with incidence rate ratios of 4.49 pre-Omicron and 1.62 during Omicron.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors concluded that hospital-acquired COVID-19 remains clinically significant, disproportionately affecting older patients and carrying higher mortality than non-hospital-acquired infection, highlighting the need for strengthened infection prevention.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform hospital infection prevention strategies by quantifying the excess mortality risk of hospital-acquired COVID-19 and showing its persistence into the Omicron era.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study’s retrospective design and reliance on surveillance data limit causal inference and generalisability, warranting moderate confidence in its conclusions.

analysis.summary_en: This retrospective cohort study in Victoria, Australia, compared hospital-acquired versus non-hospital-acquired COVID-19 across pre-Omicron and Omicron periods using linked surveillance data. Hospital-acquired cases were defined by a positive test at least eight days after admission. Among 6,485 hospital-acquired and 62,670 non-hospital-acquired episodes, median age was similar before Omicron but younger during Omicron for hospital-acquired cases. Monthly hospital-acquired cases rose to 21% under Omicron, and case fatality rates were higher for hospital-acquired cases, with incidence rate ratios of 4.49 pre-Omicron and 1.62 during Omicron. The authors conclude that hospital-acquired COVID-19 remains significant, disproportionately affecting older patients and carrying higher mortality than non-hospital-acquired infection. These findings support strengthening hospital infection prevention strategies.

title: ACE2-fused nanobody targeting a cryptic RBD epitope broadly neutralizes SARS-like viruses.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the challenge of developing broad-spectrum neutralizing agents against SARS-CoV-2 and related viruses due to their high mutation rates and cross-species transmission potential, which has compromised the effectiveness of many antibodies.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved an alternating immunization strategy in alpacas using SARS1 and SARS2 RBDs to generate cross-reactive nanobodies. Four nanobodies were identified that showed high affinities for SARS1/SARS2 RBDs and Omicron subvariants.
analysis.methods: The researchers employed an alternating immunization strategy in alpacas to generate nanobodies targeting the RBD of SARS-CoV-2 and SARS-CoV-1. They then performed structural analysis to identify the epitope targeted by the nanobody and engineered a bispecific fusion protein combining the nanobody with ACE2.
analysis.main_results: Structural analysis revealed that aSR29 targets a cryptic, highly conserved epitope at the inner base of the RBD, which is shielded from conventional antibodies by steric hindrance. This nanobody efficiently neutralizes SARS1, SARS2, and multiple Variants of Concern (VOCs), including XBB.1.5 and BQ.1.1.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted their findings as demonstrating a novel strategy for eliciting broad-spectrum nanobodies that target a hidden region of the viral spike protein, offering a potential solution for combating current and future SARS-like viruses.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that engineered nanobody–ACE2 fusions could serve as effective broad-spectrum therapeutics against emerging SARS-like viruses, providing a practical and scalable strategy for pandemic preparedness.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on abstract-only evidence, which may limit the depth of analysis. However, the reported results are grounded in structural analysis and demonstrate a clear, target-specific mechanism of action.

The researchers used an alternating immunization strategy in alpacas to generate nanobodies targeting the RBD of SARS-CoV-2 and SARS-CoV-1. The authors interpreted their findings as a novel strategy for eliciting broad-spectrum nanobodies that target a hidden region of the viral spike protein, offering a potential solution for combating current and future SARS-like viruses. The findings suggest that engineered nanobody–ACE2 fusions could serve as effective broad-spectrum therapeutics against emerging SARS-like viruses, providing a practical and scalable strategy for pandemic preparedness. title: Influenza, COVID-19, and RSV Vaccinations for Immunocompromised Children and Household Contacts.

analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on immunocompromised pediatric patients, including hematopoietic cell and solid organ transplant recipients, those undergoing chemotherapy for malignancy, and those receiving biologic response modifiers for autoimmune or inflammatory conditions, who are at risk for severe disease from vaccine-preventable respiratory viral infections such as influenza, SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19), and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). The central question is to review available data supporting current guidelines regarding vaccine dosing, scheduling, and formulations to prevent these infections in immunocompromised children.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a narrative synthesis of available data, as no specific databases, search dates, eligibility criteria, or study counts are reported. The authors aim to review existing guidelines and highlight knowledge gaps, but no systematic review or meta-analysis methodology is described.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Immunocompromised children face higher rates of hospitalization, intensive care admissions, and mortality due to severe respiratory viral infections, reflecting contributions from an immature immune system, absence of immunologic memory, and/or increased environmental exposures. Immunization recommendations for these children are largely extrapolated from studies conducted among healthy children and/or immunocompromised adults due to a paucity of primary data on immunological responses and vaccine efficacy in this population.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: There is a lack of primary data on immunological responses and vaccine efficacy specifically in immunocompromised children, leading to recommendations that are largely extrapolated from other populations. Additionally, trends in vaccine hesitancy, ongoing transmission of respiratory viral infections in the community, and suboptimal vaccination rates among immunocompromised children and their household contacts further compound the risk for this vulnerable population.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: As the number of children with immunocompromising conditions expands, it is imperative that primary care practitioners and subspecialists who care for immunocompromised children ensure appropriate immunizations are provided to these patients and their household and community contacts. The review also highlights key knowledge gaps and areas of current investigation aimed at improving respiratory viral vaccine immunogenicity and optimizing protection.

analysis.summary_en: This review addresses the increased risk of severe disease from influenza, COVID-19, and RSV in immunocompromised pediatric patients, including transplant recipients, chemotherapy patients, and those on biologic therapies. These children face higher hospitalization, ICU admission, and mortality rates due to immune system vulnerabilities and environmental exposures. Current immunization recommendations are largely extrapolated from healthy children and immunocompromised adults due to limited primary data in this population. Vaccine hesitancy, community transmission, and suboptimal vaccination rates further exacerbate risks. The review emphasizes the need for practitioners to ensure appropriate vaccinations for these patients and their contacts, while highlighting ongoing research to improve vaccine immunogenicity and protection.

title: Economic Preferences Predict COVID-19 Vaccination Intentions and Behavior.

analysis.scope_and_question: This study investigates the relationship between economic preferences and COVID-19 vaccination readiness using two representative samples of the German population (N > 5000).
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: We elicited altruism, patience, risk-taking and trust using validated survey questions.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: We find robust, positive relationships between vaccination readiness and both patience and trust.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The positive association between altruism and vaccination readiness vanishes when controlling for the other preference dimensions. No consistent effect emerges for risk-taking.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Our results underscore the importance of accounting for the interrelated nature of economic preferences when analyzing their connection with field behavior.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines how economic preferences predict COVID-19 vaccination intentions and behavior in a large German population sample. Using validated survey measures, the researchers found that patience and trust are positively associated with vaccination readiness, while altruism's effect disappears when controlling for other preferences. Risk-taking showed no consistent impact. The findings highlight the need to consider the interrelated nature of economic preferences when analyzing vaccination behavior.

title: Perceptions of Spanish-language COVID-19 video messaging among the Hispanic community: A qualitative study in the United States of America.

analysis.scope_and_question: This study explores perceptions of Spanish-language COVID-19 video messaging among the Hispanic community in the United States, focusing on how communities facing health disparities access health information about COVID-19. The central question is about the effectiveness of targeted public health messaging in improving vaccination attitudes and intentions.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The study is an interview-based qualitative analysis of 49 Hispanic individuals in a large southern suburban county. It is part of a larger three-year multi-method study and uses self-determination theory to investigate perceptions of four television-aired Spanish-language video messages on COVID-19 vaccination.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The findings indicate that human-centered, gain-frame messaging was positively received by the Hispanic community. This suggests that targeted Spanish-language public health messaging in Spanish news media could improve the quality of information about COVID-19.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The study highlights the need for more research on how to foster greater perceived resonance, credibility, and informational value of public health messages. It also suggests potential implications for psychological reactance and subsequent responses to health messaging.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The study recommends the development of more gentle suggestions for health protective behaviors in Spanish-language public health messaging. It also emphasizes the importance of understanding how communities facing health disparities access health information about COVID-19.

analysis.summary_en: This qualitative study examines the perceptions of Spanish-language video messages about COVID-19 vaccination among the Hispanic community in the United States. The research is part of a larger three-year multi-method study and uses self-determination theory to analyze the effectiveness of targeted messaging. The findings suggest that human-centered, gain-frame messaging was positively received, highlighting the need for improved Spanish-language public health communication. The study also points to the potential for more gentle suggestions to enhance the credibility and resonance of health messages, with implications for psychological reactance and public health responses. The research underscores the importance of understanding how communities with health disparities access and interpret health information.

title: Deep mutational scanning of SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid reveals regional stability patterns.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Point mutations within the SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein (NP) have the potential to impact not only detection but the viral life cycle, and therefore pathogenicity.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Leveraging deep mutational scanning (DMS) we determine the effect of 7876 (98.9%) of all possible point mutations on NP surface expression as a proxy for stability, which we term surface-expression-based folding fitness (SEBFF).
analysis.methods: We tested three computational methods to determine whether any could accurately predict the DMS data; per-variant predictions were poor, but per-site predictions were good, with machine learning methods outperforming the physics-based strategy, and ThermoMPNN-D performing most effectively with the RBD and ProteinMPNN with the DD.
analysis.main_results: We show NP susceptibility to SEBFF changes varies with region, with mutations to the structured RNA-binding domain (RBD) and dimerization domain (DD) being more likely to cause decreases in SEBFF. We show that the R203K mutation in the linker region increases the folding fitness of NP, suggesting thermostability may have been one factor driving the adoption of the R203K/G204R set of mutations arising in the alpha, gamma and omicron lineages.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Our DMS results appear consistent with the limited recombinant protein and biophysical data for NP variants available from the literature.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide insights into the functional impact of mutations in the SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein, which may inform surveillance strategies and understanding of viral evolution.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to in vitro deep mutational scanning and computational predictions, with no direct validation in viral replication systems. The evidence strength is moderate due to the comprehensive mutational coverage but lack of in vivo confirmation.

analysis.summary_en: This study used deep mutational scanning to assess the impact of 7876 point mutations on the SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein's stability, measured as surface-expression-based folding fitness (SEBFF). The results revealed regional variations in susceptibility to SEBFF changes, with the RNA-binding domain and dimerization domain being more vulnerable. Notably, the R203K mutation increased folding fitness, potentially contributing to its selection in alpha, gamma, and omicron lineages. Computational predictions showed per-site accuracy but poor per-variant performance, with machine learning methods outperforming physics-based approaches. The findings align with limited existing biophysical data and provide insights into viral evolution and mutation impacts.

title: Persistent physical and mental health effects of COVID-19 hospitalization

analysis.scope_and_question: The study investigates persistent physical and mental health effects of COVID-19 hospitalization in children, comparing outcomes during the Original/Alpha and Omicron waves, with a focus on prolonged recovery, symptoms, and psychiatric outcomes.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: A retrospective survey-based study of 176 children and families admitted to a single urban children's hospital in the Bronx, NY, USA, during the Original/Alpha wave (March 2020–March 2021) or Omicron wave (December 2021–December 2022). Psychometric assessments included PHQ-9, GAD-7, and PSC-17.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Children hospitalized during the Original/Alpha wave experienced a significantly greater burden of prolonged recovery than those during the Omicron wave. Posthospitalization symptoms were similar between COVID-positive children and uninfected controls, emphasizing the need for contemporaneous control groups. Mental health outcomes were more strongly associated with pandemic phase than infection status.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The study highlights that mental health outcomes were more linked to societal disruption than direct viral effects, but the specific mechanisms driving prolonged recovery in the Original/Alpha wave remain unclear. The role of virologic and immunologic factors in postacute physical outcomes requires further investigation.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Routine mental health screening in hospitalized children during public health emergencies is recommended. Further research is needed to understand the virologic and immunologic factors contributing to prolonged recovery in different COVID-19 waves.

analysis.summary_en: This retrospective study examines persistent health effects of COVID-19 hospitalization in children, comparing Original/Alpha and Omicron waves. Findings show prolonged recovery was more common in the Original/Alpha wave, with fatigue, shortness of breath, and sleep issues reported similarly in infected and uninfected children. Mental health outcomes were more associated with pandemic phase than infection status, suggesting societal disruption as a key factor. The study underscores the importance of control groups and recommends routine mental health screening during public health emergencies.

title: Reviewer #2 (Public review): N6-Adenosine Methylation of a Single Site in SARS-CoV-2 5′-UTR Promotes Translation

analysis.scope_and_question: The study investigates the role of N6-adenosine methylation (m6A) in the 5′-UTR of SARS-CoV-2 in promoting translation initiation, with a focus on understanding how this modification affects viral protein synthesis and its potential as a therapeutic target.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The evidence is derived from biochemical assays and bioinformatic analyses conducted on SARS-CoV-2. The study does not report specific databases, search dates, or eligibility criteria, but it describes the use of a single 5′-UTR leader for translating all 16 non-structural viral proteins from the genomic polycistronic ORFs 1a and 1b.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The study concludes that a single METTL3-dependent m6A methylation event in the SARS-CoV-2 5′-UTR regulates the rate of translation initiation. This finding is supported by the observation that the full-length 5′-UTR efficiently initiates protein translation despite its structural complexity.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The study does not report controversies or evidence gaps directly. However, it notes that the 5′-UTR's structural complexity and its role in translation initiation remain understudied, suggesting a need for further investigation into the mechanisms of m6A modification in viral RNA.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The study highlights the potential of targeting m6A modification as a novel therapeutic strategy for SARS-CoV-2. It suggests that understanding the role of m6A in viral translation could lead to the development of new treatments and interventions to combat the virus.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the role of N6-adenosine methylation (m6A) in the 5′-UTR of SARS-CoV-2 and its impact on translation initiation. The research demonstrates that a single METTL3-dependent m6A modification event in the 5′-UTR regulates the rate of protein synthesis. The findings suggest that this modification may destabilize the third stem loop (SL3) and enhance accessibility to protein complexes. These insights open new avenues for therapeutic strategies targeting SARS-CoV-2's translational mechanisms. The study emphasizes the need for further research into the biological significance of m6A modification in viral RNA and its potential applications in combating the virus.

title: The Platform trial In COVID-19 priming and BOOsting (PICOBOO): The immunogenicity, reactogenicity and safety of seven licensed COVID-19 vaccines delivered as fifth dose or subsequent boosters in immunocompetent adults.

analysis.research_question_and_background: BACKGROUND PICOBOO is a randomised, adaptive trial evaluating the immunogenicity and reactogenicity of licensed COVID-19 booster vaccines in immunocompetent individuals >12 years old.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Participants were recruited from January to November 2023 (T1) and from January to September 2024 (T2). Participants recruited during T1 were randomised to receive one of five COVID-19 booster vaccines. Participants recruited during T2 were randomised to receive one of two monovalent XBB.1.5 booster vaccines.
analysis.methods: METHODS People who had not received a booster vaccine in the three months prior were eligible. Anti-spike Immunoglobulin G (IgG) responses were evaluated in all participants. Anti-spike total Ig was evaluated in participants recruited during T1. Neutralisation responses were evaluated in a pre-defined subset.
analysis.main_results: FINDINGS There were 276 and 260 participants recruited in T1 and T2, respectively. All vaccines boosted humoral immune responses. Immunological responses measures at D28, 180 and 365 found peak total immunoglobulin (Ig), IgG and virus neutralisation (ND50) responses at D28. Responses returned to near-baseline levels by D365. Participants in the 50- < 70y-BNT162b2 stratum had higher total Ig, IgG and ND50 compared to those in the strata primed with AZD1222. The proportion who reported at least one severe event following Nvx, Pf BA.1, Mod BA.1, Pf BA.4/5, Mod BA.4/5, Pf XBB.1.5 and Mod XBB.1.5 were 1.1%, 2.9%, 6.7%, 0%, 5.9%, 2.9% and 5.4%, respectively.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: INTERPRETATION All vaccines boosted humoral immunity and had acceptable reactogenicity profiles. Higher binding and neutralising antibody responses were observed in people primed with BNT162b2.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform booster vaccine selection by demonstrating immunogenicity and safety across multiple licensed vaccines, particularly highlighting superior responses in BNT162b2-primed individuals.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's evidence strength is moderate due to its randomized design and multiple vaccine comparisons, though limitations include the absence of long-term follow-up beyond D365 and potential generalizability constraints to specific age strata.

analysis.summary_en: The PICOBOO trial evaluated the immunogenicity and reactogenicity of seven licensed COVID-19 booster vaccines as fifth doses or subsequent boosters in immunocompetent adults. Participants were stratified by age and primary vaccine schedule, with recruitment occurring in 2023 and 2024. All vaccines boosted humoral immune responses, with peak antibody levels observed at day 28 and near-baseline levels by day 365. Higher binding and neutralizing antibody responses were observed in individuals primed with BNT162b2 compared to those primed with AZD1222. Severe adverse event rates were low across all vaccine groups. The study provides evidence for booster vaccine selection, highlighting the superior immunogenicity of BNT162b2 priming and acceptable safety profiles across all evaluated vaccines.

title: Investigation of PDCD1 Gene Polymorphisms and Haplotypes in COVID-19 Severity and Outcome in a Brazilian Population.

analysis.research_question_and_background: COVID-19 severity and survival are influenced by the host immune response to SARS-CoV-2, and since genetic variability can modulate these responses, we investigated whether PDCD1 polymorphisms are associated with COVID-19 severity and mortality in a Brazilian cohort.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A total of 366 COVID-19 patients (165 mild, 72 moderate, and 129 severe cases) were genotyped for four PDCD1 SNPs, and their haplotype structures were estimated.
analysis.methods: Multinomial logistic regression identified associations between PDCD1 polymorphisms and COVID-19 severity, and haplotype analysis was performed to evaluate differences in frequencies among the groups.
analysis.main_results: Significant differences were observed in allele frequencies of rs11568821 and genotypes and allele frequencies of rs2227982 among mild, moderate, and severe cases; however, none of these associations remained independent, and no association was found between haplotypes and disease severity or outcome.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors suggest that these polymorphisms, although involved in COVID-19 immunopathogenesis, are not suitable biomarkers for predicting COVID-19 severity or clinical outcomes, and this is the first study to evaluate SNP rs2227982 in COVID-19 patients and the first to evaluate the four SNPs in a Brazilian population.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform that PDCD1 polymorphisms are not reliable biomarkers for COVID-19 severity prediction, which may guide future research toward other genetic or immunological factors for risk stratification.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence strength is moderate due to the lack of independent associations and the study's limitation to a single cohort, though the sample size and comprehensive genetic analysis provide reasonable confidence in the findings.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the association of PDCD1 gene polymorphisms with COVID-19 severity and outcome in a Brazilian cohort of 366 patients. Significant differences in allele frequencies of rs11568821 and rs2227982 were observed among mild, moderate, and severe cases, but none remained independent after multinomial logistic regression. Haplotype analysis showed no association with disease severity or outcome. The authors conclude that these polymorphisms, while involved in immunopathogenesis, are not suitable biomarkers for predicting COVID-19 severity or clinical outcomes. This is the first study to evaluate these specific SNPs in a Brazilian population, providing novel insights into genetic factors influencing COVID-19 severity.

title: "COVID Is Hard. Cancer Is Harder.": A Qualitative Study of Young Adults Diagnosed with Cancer During the COVID-19 Global Pandemic.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to explore the unique challenges faced by adolescents and young adults with cancer (AYAs) during the COVID-19 pandemic, as the pandemic compounded difficulties in accessing care, support, and managing stressors.
analysis.study_design_and_population: AYAs (ages 18-39 years) were recruited nationally, completed an online survey, and participated in one of six online focus groups from March 2022 to October 2022.
analysis.methods: Transcripts were analyzed using both deductive and inductive coding to identify themes related to AYAs' experiences of coping with a cancer diagnosis during the pandemic.
analysis.main_results: Ten AYAs who received a cancer diagnosis between 2020 and 2021 participated in focus groups; all were female and non-Hispanic White. Common themes included delays in diagnosis, restricted treatment options, compounded fear of cancer and COVID-19, psychological distress, and unexpected advantages from the pandemic.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that isolation, healthcare protocols limiting family involvement, and the emotional impacts of the pandemic created additional challenges for newly diagnosed AYAs, highlighting the need for tailored support during crises.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Findings have implications for AYAs' healthcare beyond pandemics, especially for those requiring physical isolation to manage health risks, emphasizing the need for adaptable care strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence strength is moderate due to the small sample size (n=10) and lack of diversity (all female and non-Hispanic White), limiting generalizability, though the qualitative approach provided rich insights.

analysis.summary_en: This qualitative study explored the challenges faced by adolescents and young adults (AYAs) diagnosed with cancer during the COVID-19 pandemic. Ten AYAs participated in focus groups, revealing themes of delayed diagnoses, restricted treatments, compounded fears, and psychological distress. Despite these challenges, some unexpected advantages were noted. The study highlights the additional burdens of isolation and healthcare protocols limiting family involvement, with implications for care beyond pandemics, particularly for those requiring isolation. However, the small, homogeneous sample limits generalizability.

title: Biomarkers of protection against controlled human SARS-CoV-2 Delta variant breakthrough infection

analysis.research_question_and_background: Improved understanding of how variants cause breakthrough infection, despite pre-existing immunity, is needed to advance development of next-generation SARS-CoV-2 vaccines, including those that may provide cross-variant protection or block transmission.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Healthy vaccinated adults aged 18-30 years were inoculated intranasally in a stepwise dose-escalation controlled human infection model (CHIM) with doses from 1x102 TCID50 to 1x106 TCID50 of SARS-CoV-2 Delta variant; within the 1x106 TCID50 group, participants were selected for serum neutralising antibody titres (NT50) ≤1:80.
analysis.methods: Participants were inoculated intranasally with SARS-CoV-2 Delta variant in a dose-escalation CHIM, with post-inoculation quarantine for up to 14 days and outpatient follow-up for 12 months; the primary aim was to elicit safe, well-tolerated Delta SARS-CoV-2 breakthrough infection at a rate of over 50%.
analysis.main_results: Sustained infection with mild-to-moderate symptoms occurred in 33% (6/18) of the sero-selected group; serum neutralising antibody, anti-N IgG, mucosal anti-S IgA, and N-specific T cells most strongly predicted protection from virologically-defined infection, with higher neutralisation and antibody levels correlating with lower viral load.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Susceptibility to SARS-CoV-2 breakthrough infection in those with hybrid immunity is strongly associated with low levels of pre-existing antibody, but the diversity of immune markers associated with protection implies that additional benefits may be conferred by multi-pronged immunity.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: This study establishes the framework for SARS-CoV-2 CHIM conduct, using sero-selection to increase attack rate and a process for defining quantitative correlates of protection, which is necessary for next-generation vaccine development.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was conducted in a small, young, vaccinated population with limited generalisability; however, the controlled human infection model provides high-confidence evidence for correlates of protection against Delta variant breakthrough infection.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated biomarkers of protection against SARS-CoV-2 Delta variant breakthrough infection using a controlled human infection model (CHIM) in healthy vaccinated adults aged 18-30 years. Participants were inoculated intranasally with escalating doses of Delta variant, with sero-selection for low neutralising antibody titres. The primary aim was to achieve a breakthrough infection rate of over 50%. Results showed that 33% of the sero-selected group developed sustained infection, with serum neutralising antibody, anti-N IgG, mucosal anti-S IgA, and N-specific T cells strongly predicting protection. Higher neutralisation and antibody levels correlated with lower viral load, while baseline nasal anti-S IgA was associated with lower symptom scores. The study establishes a framework for SARS-CoV-2 CHIM conduct and identifies multi-pronged immunity as beneficial for protection against breakthrough infection.

title: Modeling the public health impact of vaccination with Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine, LP.8.1, 2025–2026 formula in the pediatric population aged 5–17 years at high risk of severe outcomes from COVID-19 in the United States

analysis.study_design_and_population: A previously published static decision-tree model was adapted to compare health outcomes with and without vaccination. The study focused on the US pediatric population aged 5-17 years at high risk of severe outcomes from COVID-19.
analysis.methods: Demographic, epidemiological, vaccine (effectiveness, vaccine uptake), and clinical model inputs were derived from surveillance data and relevant published studies.
analysis.main_results: In the absence of LP.8.1-adapted BNT162b2 COVID-19 vaccination, COVID-19 burden among those aged 5-11 years and 12-17 years was projected as 1,007,114 and 1,467,724 symptomatic cases, 2,493 and 2,547 hospitalizations, and 109 and 107 COVID-19-related deaths, respectively. Increasing uptake to 50% would increase the health burden averted 6-fold.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Receipt of an LP.8.1-adapted COVID-19 vaccine was projected to reduce the COVID-19 burden in the high-risk pediatric population, even with low vaccine uptake. Increasing vaccine uptake in this population could yield larger public health impact.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that vaccination with LP.8.1-adapted BNT162b2 could significantly reduce the burden of severe outcomes in high-risk pediatric populations, highlighting the importance of increasing vaccine uptake.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study relies on a previously published static decision-tree model and assumes observed 2024-2025 uptake levels, which may limit the confidence in the projections.

analysis.summary_en: This study assesses the potential public health impact of the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine, LP.8.1, 2025-2026 formula, in the US pediatric population aged 5-17 years at high risk of severe outcomes from COVID-19. A static decision-tree model was adapted to compare health outcomes with and without vaccination. The model inputs were derived from surveillance data and published studies. The results project that without vaccination, the burden of symptomatic cases, hospitalizations, and deaths would be substantial, but vaccination could avert these cases even with low uptake. Increasing vaccine uptake is projected to yield larger public health benefits. The study's reliance on a static model and assumed uptake levels may limit the confidence in its projections. The findings suggest that vaccination could significantly reduce the burden of severe outcomes in high-risk pediatric populations, emphasizing the importance of increasing vaccine coverage.

title: SARS-CoV-2 Point-of-Care Testing Modalities: Integrating Molecular, Immunological, Biosensor, and AI Approaches

analysis.research_question_and_background: The COVID-19 pandemic highlighted the critical need for rapid, accessible, and accurate diagnostic tools to support timely clinical decision-making, outbreak control, and public health surveillance.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This review was based on a structured literature search of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science databases covering studies published between January 2020 and January 2026.
analysis.methods: Molecular POCT methods, including rapid reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR), loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP), and CRISPR-based technologies, provide high analytical sensitivity and specificity and are increasingly suitable for decentralized diagnostic applications.
analysis.main_results: The review evaluates current advances in COVID-19 POCT technologies, including molecular assays, antigen-based tests, antibody-based assays, biosensor platforms, and artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted diagnostic approaches.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings indicate that no single POCT modality is optimal for all clinical scenarios; instead, molecular, antigen, antibody, biosensor, and AI-assisted approaches provide complementary strengths that support different diagnostic and public health objectives.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Continued advances in assay design, digital connectivity, multiplex testing, and variant-resilient detection strategies are expected to further enhance the role of POCT in COVID-19 management and future infectious disease preparedness.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Emerging biosensor technologies and AI-enabled diagnostic systems demonstrate promising analytical capabilities and operational advantages; however, many remain at the prototype or early-validation stage and require further clinical evaluation before widespread implementation.

analysis.summary_en: This review examines advances in COVID-19 point-of-care testing (POCT) technologies, including molecular assays, antigen-based tests, antibody-based assays, biosensor platforms, and AI-assisted approaches. The study highlights that no single POCT modality is optimal for all clinical scenarios, as each approach offers complementary strengths for different diagnostic and public health objectives. Molecular methods like RT-PCR and LAMP provide high sensitivity and specificity, while antigen-based tests offer rapid screening. Antibody-based tests are valuable for seroprevalence studies, and emerging biosensor and AI technologies show promise but require further clinical validation. The review emphasizes the need for continued advancements in assay design, digital connectivity, and variant-resilient detection to enhance POCT's role in COVID-19 management and future pandemic preparedness.

title: Effects of COVID-19 Control Policies on Malaria Surveillance: A Comparative Analysis of North and South Korea.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Both South and North Korea are identified by the World Health Organization (WHO) as having the potential to eliminate malaria, but the increase in malaria cases during the COVID-19 response has prompted an investigation into the reasons behind this unexpected rise.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Epidemiological, entomological, and meteorological data from national and international surveillance systems were analyzed to assess drivers of malaria resurgence in North and South Korea using the WHO's analytical framework.
analysis.methods: Using the WHO's analytical framework, which can be effectively applied during the elimination phase, the study assessed drivers of malaria resurgence in North and South Korea by analyzing epidemiological, entomological, and meteorological data from national and international surveillance systems.
analysis.main_results: In North Korea, border closures caused a severe shortage of rapid diagnostic test kits, reducing malaria testing by over 90% by 2021, while confirmed cases rose from 1819 in 2020 to 3160 in 2023. In South Korea, public health resources were diverted to COVID-19, weakening malaria control activities, with response time for epidemiological investigations increasing from 1.3 days in 2019 to 4.3 days in 2021, and confirmed cases rising from 274 in 2021 to 673 in 2023.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that COVID-19-related disruptions, including supply chain failures and the diversion of human resources, impaired malaria control in countries on the Korean Peninsula, as there were no meaningful changes in the drivers of malaria resurgence, including importation of malaria parasites or human susceptibility.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform that maintaining essential health services during pandemics is crucial to prevent malaria resurgence in elimination-phase countries, highlighting the need for resilient surveillance systems and supply chains.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence strength is moderate as the study relied on surveillance data and did not include primary data collection or randomized controlled trials, with limitations including potential underreporting and the inability to establish causality definitively.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the unexpected increase in malaria cases in North and South Korea during the COVID-19 pandemic. Both countries, identified by WHO as having potential for malaria elimination, experienced resurgence. In North Korea, border closures caused a 90% reduction in malaria testing by 2021, with cases rising from 1819 in 2020 to 3160 in 2023. In South Korea, resource diversion to COVID-19 weakened malaria control, increasing investigation response time from 1.3 to 4.3 days and cases from 274 to 673 between 2021-2023. Environmental factors and resistance were not significant contributors. The study concludes that COVID-19-related disruptions impaired malaria control, emphasizing the need for resilient health systems during pandemics.

title: Low reporting quality limits the contribution of human organ models to COVID-19 research: a systematic review.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The COVID-19 pandemic created a unique situation in which researchers repurposed human models of varying complexity to investigate SARS-CoV-2, providing the opportunity to analyse their contribution across organs.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We conducted a systematic review of 558 studies, divided into pandemic and post-pandemic periods, to assess how human models were applied to investigate host factors, viral replication of SARS-CoV-2, immune responses, and to evaluate reporting quality.
analysis.methods: The study assessed how human models were applied to investigate host factors, viral replication of SARS-CoV-2, immune responses, and evaluated reporting quality through a systematic review of 558 studies.
analysis.main_results: Our analysis revealed substantial limitations that were only partially alleviated in post-pandemic studies, including heterogeneity of outcome measures, incomplete documentation of model characteristics and experimental procedures, and variable reporting quality, which were associated with reduced cross-study comparability, more difficult risk-of-bias assessment, and limited reliability and interpretability of evidence synthesis and meta-analytical results.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Strengthening community-driven reporting standards and methodological transparency is essential to enable robust evidence synthesis and to fully realise the potential of human organ models in future pandemics and translational research.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the need for improved reporting standards to enhance the reliability and interpretability of evidence from human organ models in COVID-19 research, which is crucial for future pandemic preparedness and translational research.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study identified substantial limitations in the reporting quality of human organ models used in COVID-19 research, including heterogeneity of outcome measures, incomplete documentation, and variable reporting quality, which reduced cross-study comparability and limited the reliability of evidence synthesis; the evidence strength is moderate due to the systematic review approach but is constrained by these reporting limitations.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review analyzed 558 studies on human organ models used in COVID-19 research, divided into pandemic and post-pandemic periods. The study assessed how these models were applied to investigate host factors, viral replication, and immune responses, while evaluating reporting quality. Findings revealed substantial limitations, including heterogeneity in outcome measures, incomplete documentation of model characteristics and procedures, and variable reporting quality. These issues reduced cross-study comparability, complicated risk-of-bias assessment, and limited the reliability of evidence synthesis and meta-analytical results. The authors emphasize that strengthening community-driven reporting standards and methodological transparency is essential to fully realize the potential of human organ models in future pandemics and translational research.

title: Long-term Cardiovascular Outcomes in US Medicare Beneficiaries After COVID-19 Hospitalization During the Omicron Era.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the knowledge gap regarding long-term cardiovascular outcomes in older adults hospitalized with COVID-19 during the Omicron era, as prior data from the pre-Omicron era indicated an increased risk of major adverse cardiovascular events.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective cohort study was conducted on Medicare beneficiaries aged ≥65 years hospitalized for COVID-19 during the Omicron era (November 2021-September 2022), the pre-Omicron era (March 2020-November 2021), and a historical influenza cohort (October 2017-September 2018).
analysis.methods: The study used inverse probability weighting to standardize the cohorts and compared the risk of death and major adverse cardiovascular events between the Omicron and pre-Omicron cohorts, as well as the influenza cohort.
analysis.main_results: The primary outcome, a composite of all-cause death and cardiovascular events, occurred in 48.8% of the Omicron cohort, 49.3% of the pre-Omicron cohort, and 33.4% of the influenza cohort. The Omicron cohort had a significantly lower risk of death (34.2% vs. 39.7%) but a higher risk of myocardial infarction, stroke, pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis, and heart failure compared to the pre-Omicron cohort.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that the risk of death was lower in the Omicron era than in the pre-Omicron era, but the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events was higher, highlighting a shift in the post-hospitalization outcomes associated with SARS-CoV-2 variants.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that cardiovascular prevention strategies should be prioritized for older adults recovering from Omicron-related COVID-19 hospitalizations, as the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events remains elevated compared to influenza.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and potential for confounding factors, but the evidence is strong due to the large sample size and standardized cohort comparison.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated long-term cardiovascular outcomes in older adults hospitalized with COVID-19 during the Omicron era compared to the pre-Omicron era and a historical influenza cohort. It found that while the risk of death was lower in the Omicron era, the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events was higher than in the pre-Omicron era. The results emphasize the need for targeted cardiovascular prevention strategies post-COVID-19 hospitalization, particularly for those affected by the Omicron variant. The study's large sample size and standardized cohort comparison provide strong evidence, though limitations include the retrospective design and potential confounding factors.

title: Persistence of SARS-CoV-2 RNA Residues in Placenta Tissue Following Maternal COVID-19 Infection During Pregnancy.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Prolonged SARS-CoV-2 viral persistence was reported in extrapulmonary tissues in patients infected with COVID-19, but little is known about SARS-CoV-2 viral persistence in the placenta.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This is a retrospective and IRB approved study analyzing placental tissue samples from 40 women infected with COVID-19 at various gestational age.
analysis.methods: SARS-CoV-2 RNA expression was examined by in situ hybridization on placental disk and fetal membrane, S-protein and N-protein expression was determined by immunostaining, and SARS-CoV-2 RNA sequencing was performed in 12 out of the 29 cases with positive RNA detection.
analysis.main_results: SARS-CoV-2 RNA expression was detected in placental disk, predominantly localized in syncytiotrophoblasts in 29 out of the 40 cases, with the longest interval from infection to delivery being 221 days; viral RNA expression was also detected in villous core vessel endothelium in two COVID (+) newborn placentas.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: These findings provide compelling evidence that SARS-CoV-2 genetic material can persist in placental tissue long after maternal infection, potentially contributing to a sustained inflammatory environment at the maternal-fetal interface during pregnancy.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The persistence of SARS-CoV-2 RNA in placental tissue may have implications for understanding the long-term effects of COVID-19 on pregnancy outcomes and fetal development, warranting further investigation into potential clinical monitoring strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and the absence of S-protein and N-protein expression in most cases, though the detection of partial RdRp sequence provides a possible explanation for undetectable protein expression; the evidence strength is moderate due to the sample size and methodological constraints.

analysis.summary_en: This retrospective study investigated SARS-CoV-2 viral persistence in placental tissue from 40 women infected with COVID-19 at various gestational ages. Using in situ hybridization, immunostaining, and RNA sequencing, the researchers detected SARS-CoV-2 RNA in 29 out of 40 placental disk samples, predominantly in syncytiotrophoblasts, with the longest interval from infection to delivery being 221 days. Notably, 57.9% of cases with negative COVID-19 tests at delivery still showed viral RNA expression. While S-protein and N-protein expression was undetectable in most cases, partial RdRp sequences were identified, suggesting viral persistence without active protein production. The findings indicate that SARS-CoV-2 genetic material can persist in placental tissue long after maternal infection, potentially contributing to sustained inflammation at the maternal-fetal interface.
